analysis.one_liner: Forces the big freight railroads to quote rates, open tracks to competitors, and arbitrate captive-shipper disputes.
analysis.headline: The Railroad Competition Act of 2006 had no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targeted the small group of giant freight railroads that dominate U.S. rail shipping. In many regions — especially farm country — a single big railroad is the only one serving a customer, so it can charge premium rates with little fear of competition. The bill would have required railroads to quote a rate between any two points on request, opened their tracks to competing railroads, sent rate and service disputes to arbitration on a fast timetable, made it easier for shippers to challenge high rates using the railroad's actual costs, and created a federal "Rail Customer Advocate" inside the Agriculture Department to speak for farm and timber shippers.
analysis.who_benefits: Captive rail customers — farmers, grain elevators, timber and paper companies, utilities, and other businesses that depend on one big railroad and pay above-competitive rates — plus, indirectly, consumers, since high freight costs feed into food, energy, and goods prices.

how_it_helps.text: Required a railroad, on a shipper's request, to quote a rate and provide service between any two points on its system, regardless of the shipper's other contracts or arrangements.

Changed the Surface Transportation Board's power to require reciprocal switching — letting a shipper served by one railroad hand cars to a competing railroad's tracks — from optional to mandatory, and barred the board from demanding proof of anticompetitive conduct first.

Created "areas of inadequate rail competition" for regions or commodities served by only one Class I railroad, unlocking remedies like competitor access, haulage at board-set fees, and expedited rate review.
Required rail rate and service disputes to go to arbitration if the non-railroad party elects it, with decisions due within 120 to 180 days.

Directed the board to adopt a rate-review method based on the railroad's actual costs, and barred it from using hypothetical-competitor cost methods, which historically made shipper rate challenges slow and expensive.

Established an Office of Rail Customer Advocacy in the Department of Agriculture to represent agricultural and forestry shippers in board proceedings, with a study and report on how well the remedies work for smaller shippers.
Required the board to post rail service complaints on its website within 7 days and file an annual report to Congress on complaints against each Class I railroad.

analysis.who_pays: The big Class I freight railroads — the handful of companies (such as Union Pacific, BNSF, CSX, and Norfolk Southern) that control most U.S. rail freight — would give up premium rates on captive traffic and cede track access to competitors. Railroads argue this cuts revenue available for track and equipment investment, and any new office is funded by taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: The big Class I freight railroads

drawbacks.text: The bill would channel many rate and service disputes into binding arbitration rather than open regulatory or court proceedings, limiting the kind of precedent-setting review that benefits future shippers.

Its arbitration and competition-design provisions guarantee railroads a floor of 180 percent of variable costs — a substantial profit margin — even while providing "relief" to captive shippers, so the bill would lock in high railroad profitability alongside lower disputes.

Mandated competitor access to railroad tracks and forced rate quotes could reduce the incentive of the companies that own the tracks to invest in them — the standard objection railroads and their allies raised to such proposals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is sound for its purpose: it attacks a real problem — a few consolidated railroads charging premium rates to customers with no alternative — with concrete remedies rather than studies. Its biggest concessions are to the industry itself: the 180-percent cost floor and binding arbitration protect railroad margins and narrow shipper recourse. On balance it would likely have shifted money from railroads to captive shippers and consumers, with some risk of reduced investment incentives.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2006 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Dayton of Minnesota introduced the Railroad Competition Act of 2006 on May 22, 2006, with Senate Democratic Leader Harry Reid introducing it on his behalf.
Not a single senator cosponsored the bill, from either party.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The big Class I freight railroads came out ahead: they kept their pricing power over captive shippers and faced no rate, access, or arbitration mandates, while captive customers — farmers and rural shippers paying above-competitive rates — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big freight railroads kept pricing power

for.name: Mark Dayton
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to boost rail competition for captive shippers.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Dayton's behalf on the Senate floor.

against.name: Ted Stevens
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never brought the bill to a hearing, markup, or vote after its referral; the record shows no committee action.

against.name: Class I freight railroads
against.role: Consolidated industry controlling most U.S. rail freight
against.what_they_did: Long opposed reciprocal switching mandates and rate regulation of captive traffic, which this bill would have imposed.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic sponsor drew no cosponsors from either party and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have cut into the premium rates these consolidated railroads charge customers with no competing railroad, and opened their tracks to rivals. That pricing power is the direct cost borne by shippers and, through freight costs, by consumers.
Grain, farm-supply, and timber shippers often depend on a single railroad; the bill gave them guaranteed rate quotes, arbitration, competitor access, and a dedicated USDA advocate.

industries.industry: Other captive rail customers (utilities, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: Coal, chemical, and industrial customers served by one railroad would have gained expedited rate review using the railroad's actual costs and access to fast arbitration.
